summary: Defines SNMP managed objects used to manage devices that run Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP), a protocol for exchanging routing information about telephony destinations between location servers.

eli5.summary: This gives network managers a standard set of dials for checking on devices that help phone calls find their way over the internet.

subtitle: The SNMP objects for monitoring and configuring Telephony Routing over IP location servers.

tldr.problem: Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP) location servers exchange routing information between domains, and operators need a standard way to configure and monitor them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3872 defines a MIB module and a textual conventions module, modeled on the BGP-4 MIB, with tables for configuration, peers, routes and statistics, and notifications for session events.
tldr.outcome: Operators can manage TRIP location servers through SNMP, and RFC 3872 recommends SNMPv3 security because some objects are sensitive.

today: RFC 3872 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2004, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the MIB definition for TRIP as written here.

sections.title: What the TRIP MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 3872 defines Management Information Base (MIB) modules for managing devices that run Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP), which is defined in RFC 3219. TRIP is an inter-domain application-layer control protocol that exchanges information between TRIP location servers (LS) to provide efficient IP telephony routing.

The modules use SMIv2 and are meant to be read through SNMP. Because TRIP is modeled after BGP-4, the managed objects are modeled after the BGP-4 MIB of RFC 1657.
sections.eli5: TRIP is how phone routing computers tell each other where numbers can be reached. This document lists the standard questions a manager can ask those computers.

sections.title: How the MIB Is Organized
sections.content:
The MIB uses the framework of RFC 2788, so one system can manage several TRIP instances. The Network Services Monitoring MIB applTable gets an entry per TRIP Location Server, and each gets an applIndex that identifies that instance.

Seven groups divide the work: configuration, peer configuration, routes, ITAD topology, peer statistics, notifications, and the objects that notifications need. The objects in the configuration table SHOULD be non-volatile and survive a reboot. The RFC registers the MIB module under mib-2 116 and the textual conventions module under mib-2 115.
sections.eli5: The control panel is split into drawers: settings, friends you talk to, routes you know, maps, counters and alarms. Each phone-routing machine gets its own numbered panel.

sections.title: Tables and Textual Conventions
sections.content:
A separate textual conventions module defines shared types. TripItad identifies an IP Telephony Administrative Domain. TripId is a 4-octet unsigned integer that identifies a location server within its ITAD. It may represent an IPv4 address but never an IPv6 address. Other conventions cover the address family, the application protocol, the community identifier, the protocol version and the send/receive mode.

The main module has a configuration table (version, ITAD, identifier, admin and operational status, address, port, intervals, send and receive mode), a peer table, a peer statistics table, a route table with a community table, and ITAD topology tables. Route entries record which Telephony Routing Information Base (TRIB) they belong to, using a bit map: adjTribIns, extTrib, locTrib and adjTribOut.
sections.eli5: Some labels, like a phone-network ID, are used in many places, so they are defined once in a shared glossary page that every table points to.

sections.title: Peer States
sections.content:
The tripPeerState object reports the state of the TRIP finite state machine for a peer. idle is the initial state, where the local LS refuses all incoming connections. In connect it waits for a transport connection to complete, and in active it listens for an inbound connection without initiating one. In openSent it has sent an OPEN message and waits for one back. In openConfirm it has sent and received OPEN messages, and has answered with a KEEPALIVE. In established the LS can exchange UPDATE, NOTIFICATION and KEEPALIVE messages.

The write-able tripPeerAdminStatus controls the connection: up allows it, and down disconnects and blocks further connections, which forces the state to idle.
sections.eli5: Two machines meeting go through steps: not talking, knocking on the door, introducing themselves, then chatting for as long as they like.

sections.title: Statistics and Notifications
sections.content:
The peer statistics table counts updates and total messages sent and received, and records how many times the session reached the established state, along with the time spent established and the time of the last state change.

Nine SNMP notifications report events. tripConnectionEstablished fires on entering the established state, and tripConnectionDropped on leaving it. Others report FSM errors, OPEN and UPDATE message errors, an expired hold timer, a connection collision when two location servers try to connect to each other at once, a peer's Cease message, and errors in a TRIP notification message. The RFC notes that this last one is a TRIP protocol message, not an SNMP notification.
sections.eli5: The machines keep score of how many messages they sent and ring a bell when a friend connects, disconnects, or something goes wrong.

sections.title: Security of the Objects
sections.content:
Writable objects can harm the network if set improperly. For example, a wrong tripCfgItad can make all peer connections drop and not be re-established, setting tripCfgAdminStatus to down stops message processing, and a wrong tripCfgPort can stop peers from connecting. Bad hold time or keepalive values can make peer sessions more fragile and less resilient to denial of service attacks.

Some objects reveal sensitive information, such as a location server's addresses, so even read access should be controlled. SNMPv1 alone is not a secure environment. The RFC RECOMMENDS the SNMPv3 security features and says that deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The dials can break things if turned the wrong way, and the readouts show private details. So only trusted people should get the panel, and the connection to it should be protected.
